steps.body: Partial products write those four regions as four lines, then add them. The layout changes; the mathematics does not.
steps.narration: Partial products write those four regions as four lines, then add them. The layout changes; the mathematics does not.

widget.prompt: Build 26 × 18 as a rectangle: 26 wide and 18 tall.
widget.successFeedback: 468 — the sum of 200, 160, 60 and 48, the four partial products.
widget.lowFeedback: Smaller than 468 — both sides must reach the full factors.
widget.highFeedback: Larger than 468 — a side has overshot.
widget.factorFeedback: That area is right, but built from other sides — the model asked for is 26 across and 18 down.

predict.prompt: In 26 × 18, what is the LARGEST partial product?
predict.reveal: The tens-by-tens region is by far the biggest piece — which is why dropping it is the costliest mistake.

cml.actionGoal: Split a factor into places, build each piece, and reassemble the whole for g4m 2x2 partial.
invariants: Splitting a factor never changes the product: every piece of the split multiplies the other factor, and the pieces add back to exactly the same total, which is what makes g4m 2x2 partial decomposable at all.
misconceptions: Adding only some of the partial products, dropping or inventing a zero when factors carry tens, or letting a remainder reach or exceed the divisor.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: If one partial product were left out, exactly how much of the total would go missing?

widget.prompt: Use an area model for 32 × 13. What is the product?

commonErrors.feedback: That added only the corner pieces — the two middle rectangles were left out of the total.
That is only the tens row of the model; the ones row still has to join it.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Split a factor into its places, multiply each part, and add every piece back.

widget.prompt: Which four partial products build the area model for 38 × 15?

options.feedback: Correct — both factors split, so the rectangle has four regions and every pairing appears once.

options.label: 30×10 and 8×5
options.feedback: Only the two corner regions. The 30×5 and 8×10 rectangles are real area too.

options.label: 38×10 and 38×5
options.feedback: That splits only one factor — a valid method, but not the FOUR-region model this asks for.
Two of those multiply a factor's own pieces together, which no side of the rectangle measures.
